lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 1.

items.signText:
Please label all your food in the fridge with your name and the date you are leaving. Any food without a label will be thrown away on Monday mornings.
FREE SHELF: help yourself to anything here!
items.question: What does the note tell guests?
options: a) All food in the fridge is removed every Monday.
b) They can take any food they find in the fridge.
c) They should write their departure date on their food.
items.explanation: Guests must label food 'with your name and the date you are leaving'. Only the free shelf is for everyone – not the whole fridge – and only 'food without a label' is thrown away on Mondays, not all food.

items.signText: Hi Tom, we've arrived, but the field by the river is flooded, so we've put our tent in the top field next to the shower block instead. Look for the green tent. Bring a torch – it's really dark up here! Ellie
items.question: Why has Ellie sent this message?
options: a) To ask Tom to buy a new torch on the way
b) To warn Tom not to go near the river
c) To tell Tom where to find her
items.explanation: Ellie explains that they are 'in the top field next to the shower block' and tells Tom to 'Look for the green tent', so she is telling him where they are. She asks him to 'Bring a torch', not to buy one, and she mentions the flooded field only to explain why they moved.

items.signText: Sheets and pillowcases are included in the price of your bed. Towels can be hired from reception for £2. On the morning you leave, please put your used sheets in the basket by the front door.
items.question: What does the sign say?
options: a) The price of a bed includes the use of a towel.
b) Guests should leave their sheets in a basket.
c) Guests need to bring their own sheets.
items.explanation: The sign says 'please put your used sheets in the basket by the front door' on the day you leave. Sheets are 'included in the price', so guests do not bring their own, but towels cost '£2' extra, so they are not included.

items.signText:
Dear Ms Lindqvist,
Thank you for booking a pitch for 14–16 August. Please note that reception closes at 8 pm. If you expect to arrive later, call us before 6 pm and we will leave your welcome pack in the box by the gate.
Glenmore Farm Campsite
items.question: What should Ms Lindqvist do if she will arrive after 8 pm?
options: a) Wait at the gate until someone comes
b) Phone the campsite earlier that day
c) Collect her welcome pack from reception
items.explanation: The email says 'If you expect to arrive later, call us before 6 pm'. Reception is closed after 8 pm, so she cannot collect the pack there – it will be 'in the box by the gate' – and the email does not say that anyone will come to the gate.

items.signText:
QUIET TIME: 10.30 pm – 7 am
No music or loud voices in the camping fields.
The gate is locked during these hours, so cars cannot enter or leave the site.
items.question: What does the sign say?
options: a) Campers can't drive in or out late at night.
b) Campers must be inside their tents by 10.30 pm.
c) Cars must be parked outside the campsite at night.
items.explanation: Between 10.30 pm and 7 am 'The gate is locked … so cars cannot enter or leave the site'. Cars are not sent outside the site – they just cannot move in or out – and the sign only asks for no music or loud voices, not for people to be in their tents.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 3.
lesenParts.text:
On a wet Saturday evening in October, Rhys Evans was halfway through dinner with his family when his phone made a sound he knows very well. A walker had fallen on a mountain path above the village and couldn't stand up. Within ten minutes Rhys had left his food, put on his boots and was driving to the team's base.

Rhys, 38, runs a bicycle shop in north Wales. He is also one of around forty volunteers in the local mountain rescue team, and none of them is paid. 'People are often amazed when I tell them that,' he says. 'They imagine we're professionals working for the government. In fact, we're teachers, farmers, nurses, and one of us is a dentist.' The team depends on money from the public to buy everything from ropes to its two vehicles.

Rhys joined eight years ago, after he got lost himself. 'I'd gone up a mountain in trainers, without a map, and the cloud came down,' he remembers, smiling. 'I'm embarrassed about it now. The team found me in about an hour, and they didn't make me feel stupid at all. I decided I wanted to do the same for other people.'

Becoming a member wasn't quick. New volunteers train for about a year before they go out on real rescues, learning first aid, how to use ropes and how to find their way at night. Rhys admits he nearly gave up. 'I thought I was fit, but carrying a heavy stretcher down a steep hill in the rain is something else. I was always the slowest.' What kept him going, he says, was the support of the older members, who never criticised him.

The team is called out more than a hundred times a year, and the number is growing. Rhys believes social media is partly responsible. 'Someone posts a beautiful photo from the top of a mountain, and thousands of people want to go there. Many of them have no idea how quickly the weather can change.' However, he doesn't want people to stay away. 'We'd much rather people came well prepared, with warm clothes, a map and a charged phone, than not at all.'

That October night, the walker turned out to have a broken ankle. It took the team four hours to carry her down. Rhys got home after two in the morning and opened his shop as usual at nine. Is it worth it? 'Every time,' he says.

questions.question: What often surprises people about the mountain rescue team?
questions.explanation: Rhys says the volunteers are not paid: 'none of them is paid. People are often amazed when I tell them that.' People wrongly 'imagine we're professionals working for the government', and the team actually 'depends on money from the public'. The number of call-outs and the ten-minute journey are facts in the text, but nothing says they surprise people.
options: a) How quickly its members can get to the base
b) That its members receive no money for their work
c) That it is organised and paid for by the government
d) How many times it is called out every year

questions.question: Why did Rhys decide to join the team?
questions.explanation: When Rhys was lost, 'The team found me in about an hour, and they didn't make me feel stupid at all. I decided I wanted to do the same for other people.' He is embarrassed about going up 'in trainers, without a map', not about his fitness, and no friend or wish to improve his own skills is mentioned.
options: a) He wanted to improve his own skills in the mountains.
b) He was grateful for the way the team had helped him.
c) A friend who was already a member asked him to join.
d) He felt embarrassed that he was not fit enough.

questions.question: What did Rhys find most difficult during his training?
questions.explanation: Rhys says: 'I thought I was fit, but carrying a heavy stretcher down a steep hill in the rain is something else. I was always the slowest.' Finding the way at night and first aid are part of the training, but he does not say they were hard, and the older members 'never criticised him'.
options: a) The physical effort of carrying people down
b) Learning how to find his way in the dark
c) The comments he got from the older members
d) Finding enough free time to study first aid

questions.question: What is Rhys's opinion about people who go walking in the mountains?
questions.explanation: Rhys 'doesn't want people to stay away' and says: 'We'd much rather people came well prepared, with warm clothes, a map and a charged phone, than not at all.' He thinks social media is 'partly responsible' for more call-outs, but he does not ask people to stop posting, and he never says only experienced walkers should go.
options: a) Fewer people should go there because it is dangerous.
b) Walkers should stop sharing photos on social media.
c) Only experienced walkers should try to climb the high mountains.
d) Anyone can go if they take the right things with them.

questions.question: What is the writer mainly trying to do in this article?
questions.explanation: The article follows Rhys from the call during dinner, through his reasons for joining and his training, to opening 'his shop as usual at nine' after a night rescue, so it shows what being a volunteer involves. The October rescue, money from the public and safety equipment are each mentioned only briefly as part of his story.
options: a) Describe how one injured walker was rescued at night
b) Explain why rescue teams need more money
c) Show what life is like for a rescue volunteer
d) Give advice on staying safe in the mountains

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 4.
lesenParts.text:
When Sophie Marsh emptied her kitchen bin one evening in January, she counted the plastic inside: fourteen bags, nine food trays and a broken toy. 'That was just two days' rubbish for a family of four,' she says. (1) ________ Their two children, aged eight and eleven, were much less enthusiastic.

The first weeks were the hardest. Almost everything in their usual supermarket came wrapped in plastic, from cucumbers to cheese. (2) ________ Some of the stallholders found this strange at first, but most were happy to help.

Food was not the only problem. Shampoo, toothpaste and washing-up liquid all came in plastic bottles. (3) ________ Her homemade toothpaste, she admits, was not a success. 'It tasted like salty chalk,' laughs her son, Leo.

Living without plastic also took a lot of time. Dan worked out that the family spent about four extra hours a week shopping and cooking. (4) ________ By the end of the year, their food bills had fallen by almost a fifth.

The experiment ended last December. The family did not manage to avoid plastic completely, because some things, such as medicines, were impossible to buy without it. But their rubbish fell from two full bins a week to one small bag a month. (5) ________ Leo, who complained the most at the beginning, now gives talks about it at his school.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (1)?
questions.explanation: 'It was then' refers to the evening when Sophie counted the plastic, 'it' means plastic, and the decision made by 'she and her husband' contrasts with the next sentence: 'Their two children… were much less enthusiastic.' The sentence saying the children were 'delighted' contradicts 'much less enthusiastic'.
options: A) On the other hand, they saved money, because they stopped buying ready meals and snacks.
B) It was then that she and her husband, Dan, decided to try living without it for a whole year.
C) The children were delighted and helped to plan every detail.
D) Luckily, their local supermarket had already stopped selling food in plastic.
E) So the family started doing their shopping at the weekly market in Norwich, taking their own bags and boxes.
F) Cooking every meal from fresh ingredients, however, took hardly any time at all.
G) Even the children now refuse to go back to their old habits.
H) Sophie solved this by learning to make some of them herself, using recipes she found online.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (2)?
questions.explanation: Because the supermarket's food 'came wrapped in plastic', the family went to 'the weekly market' with 'their own bags and boxes'. The next sentence, 'Some of the stallholders found this strange', needs the market to have been mentioned. The sentence saying the supermarket had stopped selling food in plastic contradicts 'Almost everything in their usual supermarket came wrapped in plastic'.
options: A) On the other hand, they saved money, because they stopped buying ready meals and snacks.
B) It was then that she and her husband, Dan, decided to try living without it for a whole year.
C) The children were delighted and helped to plan every detail.
D) Luckily, their local supermarket had already stopped selling food in plastic.
E) So the family started doing their shopping at the weekly market in Norwich, taking their own bags and boxes.
F) Cooking every meal from fresh ingredients, however, took hardly any time at all.
G) Even the children now refuse to go back to their old habits.
H) Sophie solved this by learning to make some of them herself, using recipes she found online.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (3)?
questions.explanation: 'This' is the problem of shampoo and toothpaste in 'plastic bottles', and 'some of them' are those products. Making them herself leads to the next sentence: 'Her homemade toothpaste, she admits, was not a success.' No other sentence explains why her toothpaste was 'homemade'.
options: A) On the other hand, they saved money, because they stopped buying ready meals and snacks.
B) It was then that she and her husband, Dan, decided to try living without it for a whole year.
C) The children were delighted and helped to plan every detail.
D) Luckily, their local supermarket had already stopped selling food in plastic.
E) So the family started doing their shopping at the weekly market in Norwich, taking their own bags and boxes.
F) Cooking every meal from fresh ingredients, however, took hardly any time at all.
G) Even the children now refuse to go back to their old habits.
H) Sophie solved this by learning to make some of them herself, using recipes she found online.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (4)?
questions.explanation: 'On the other hand' contrasts the extra time ('four extra hours a week') with a benefit, and saving money leads to the next sentence: 'their food bills had fallen by almost a fifth.' The sentence saying cooking 'took hardly any time at all' contradicts 'Living without plastic also took a lot of time'.
options: A) On the other hand, they saved money, because they stopped buying ready meals and snacks.
B) It was then that she and her husband, Dan, decided to try living without it for a whole year.
C) The children were delighted and helped to plan every detail.
D) Luckily, their local supermarket had already stopped selling food in plastic.
E) So the family started doing their shopping at the weekly market in Norwich, taking their own bags and boxes.
F) Cooking every meal from fresh ingredients, however, took hardly any time at all.
G) Even the children now refuse to go back to their old habits.
H) Sophie solved this by learning to make some of them herself, using recipes she found online.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (5)?
questions.explanation: After the good result, 'Even the children now refuse to go back to their old habits', and the next sentence gives an example: 'Leo, who complained the most at the beginning, now gives talks about it.' The sentence saying the children were delighted from the start contradicts 'complained the most at the beginning'.
options: A) On the other hand, they saved money, because they stopped buying ready meals and snacks.
B) It was then that she and her husband, Dan, decided to try living without it for a whole year.
C) The children were delighted and helped to plan every detail.
D) Luckily, their local supermarket had already stopped selling food in plastic.
E) So the family started doing their shopping at the weekly market in Norwich, taking their own bags and boxes.
F) Cooking every meal from fresh ingredients, however, took hardly any time at all.
G) Even the children now refuse to go back to their old habits.
H) Sophie solved this by learning to make some of them herself, using recipes she found online.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 5.
lesenParts.text:
Today almost everyone carries a mobile phone, but the first ones looked very different. In 1983, one of the earliest mobile phones (1) ____ on sale in the United States. It weighed nearly a kilogram, its battery lasted for (2) ____ thirty minutes, and it cost almost four thousand dollars.

During the 1990s, phones became smaller and cheaper, and people started sending text messages. At first, each message could only (3) ____ up to 160 characters, so users invented short forms like "CU L8R" for "see you later".

The biggest change came in 2007, when smartphones with large touch screens became popular. Suddenly people could take photos, listen to music and search the internet without (4) ____ a computer. Within a few years, these phones had (5) ____ the place of cameras, maps and even alarm clocks for millions of people.

Some experts are worried that we now spend too much time looking at our screens. However, it is hard to (6) ____ life without these clever little machines, and they will probably continue to change in ways we cannot yet predict.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (1).
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "go on sale", meaning become available to buy: the phone "went on sale in the United States". 'Put on sale' would need a passive ('was put on sale'), and 'made' or 'set on sale' are not used.
options: a) went
b) made
c) set
d) put

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (2).
questions.explanation: The battery "lasted for only thirty minutes": 'only' goes before a number to show it is small. 'Alone', 'single' and 'unique' cannot be used before 'thirty minutes' in this way.
options: a) alone
b) single
c) unique
d) only

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (3).
questions.explanation: Each message "could only contain up to 160 characters", meaning it could have no more than 160 letters and symbols in it. 'Consist' and 'belong' need a preposition (consist of, belong to), and 'involve' means 'include as a necessary activity', which does not fit characters in a message.
options: a) contain
b) belong
c) involve
d) consist

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (4).
questions.explanation: People could "search the internet without using a computer", because the phone itself did the job. 'Making a computer' means building one, and 'doing' or 'spending a computer' are not possible.
options: a) spending
b) using
c) making
d) doing

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (5).
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "take the place of", meaning replace: smartphones "had taken the place of cameras, maps and even alarm clocks". 'Given', 'put' and 'made the place of' are not English expressions.
options: a) made
b) given
c) put
d) taken

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (6).
questions.explanation: "It is hard to imagine life without these clever little machines" means it is difficult to picture life with no phones. 'Think' and 'wonder' need a preposition or clause ('think about', 'wonder what…'), and 'believe life without' does not make sense.
options: a) believe
b) wonder
c) imagine
d) think

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 6.
lesenParts.text:
Last winter our cat, Biscuit, disappeared. He always comes home for his dinner at six o'clock, so when he didn't appear, we started to worry.

We searched the garden and the street with torches, but by midnight we (1) ____ still not found him anywhere. The next day my sister made posters with his photo, and we put them on every lamp post in the neighbourhood. Several people called, but none of the cats they had seen was Biscuit.

By Thursday, Biscuit had been missing (2) ____ Sunday evening, and we were starting to give (3) ____ hope. Then, at ten o'clock that night, our neighbour Mr Davies knocked on the door. He had been clearing out his garage and had heard a quiet noise behind some old paint tins.

I ran next door as fast (4) ____ I could. There was Biscuit, dusty and (5) ____ thin that I hardly recognised him. He must have walked into the garage while the door was open and got trapped.

It wasn't (6) ____ he had eaten two bowls of food that he finally began to purr. Now we always check Mr Davies's garage first!

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (1).
questions.explanation: By midnight points to a time in the past, so the past perfect is needed: "by midnight we had still not found him anywhere". Have would need a present time.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (2).
questions.explanation: With a perfect tense, 'since' introduces the point in time when something started: "Biscuit had been missing since Sunday evening". 'For' is used with a period of time (for four days), not with a point like 'Sunday evening'.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (3).
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'give up hope' means stop believing something good will happen: after four days "we were starting to give up hope".

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (4).
questions.explanation: The comparison 'as + adverb + as' needs a second 'as': "I ran next door as fast as I could".

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (5).
questions.explanation: The pattern is 'so + adjective + that' to show a result: Biscuit was "so thin that I hardly recognised him". 'Such' is not possible before an adjective without a noun, and 'too' cannot be followed by 'that'.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (6).
questions.explanation: The pattern 'It wasn't until … that …' shows that something happened only after another event: "It wasn't until he had eaten two bowls of food that he finally began to purr." 'Till' has the same meaning and is also accepted.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 1.
horenParts.transcript:
Man: What's happening on Saturday, Lily? You've got your dance class in the morning, haven't you?
Lily: Not this week. The teacher's on holiday. And I've been invited to Zara's birthday party, but it's at the same time as the riding lesson Grandma booked for me.
Man: So which one will you go to?
Lily: Well, Grandma's already paid for the lesson, so I'll do that and send Zara a present.

Woman: Did you go camping with your brother at the weekend, Alex?
Alex: That was the plan, but the weather was awful, so we stayed in town.
Woman: Oh no. What did you do instead?
Alex: Well, we wanted to go to the food festival in the park, but that was cancelled because of the rain as well. So we went to the transport museum. It was much better than I expected, actually.

Nina: So where shall we meet for the film tomorrow, Chloe?
Chloe: It starts at seven. Shall we meet outside the cinema at quarter to?
Nina: It's going to rain all evening, according to the forecast. Why don't we meet in the café next door? We can have a hot chocolate first.
Chloe: Good idea. I'm getting the bus, so I'll come straight from the bus station. See you there at half six.

Woman: You're not going to play that computer game all evening again, are you, Ethan?
Ethan: No, I'm bored of it. Kieran asked me to go bowling, but it costs twelve pounds and I've only got five.
Woman: So you're staying in?
Ethan: Yes, but the big match is on TV at eight, and I really want to see that. Can I invite Kieran round to watch it?

Rachel: I've booked tickets for the theme park in the half-term holiday.
Chris: Great. Did you get the family ticket?
Rachel: I looked at that, but it's only for two adults and two children, and we're taking your mum as well. And the one-day tickets were thirty pounds each! So I got the tickets for the whole year. They cost a bit more, but if we go twice, they're cheaper.

Man: And now some news for music fans. The Greenfield Music Festival is back in August, but not in its usual place by the river, because the field there is still too wet after the floods in the spring. The organisers wanted to use the beach, but the town council said no. So this year it'll be in the grounds of Harwood Castle, which is only a short bus ride from the town centre.

Woman: I can't believe you got tickets for the Blue Lights concert! They sold out online in ten minutes.
Dan: I know. I tried the website as soon as they went on sale, but it kept crashing. Then I thought about queuing at the box office, but people were there all night.
Woman: So how did you get them?
Dan: My friend Tariq won two in a radio competition, and he can't go, so he gave them to me.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 2.
horenParts.transcript:
Fiona: I read that we should all sleep eight hours a night. I'm lucky if I get six.
Dominic: Me too. I always look at my phone in bed, and then I'm awake for ages.
Fiona: Same here. I really think the screen keeps you awake. I'm going to leave mine in the kitchen.
Dominic: Good idea. Mind you, I went swimming yesterday and I still couldn't sleep.
Fiona: Really? Swimming always makes me sleep like a baby.

Gareth: How's the new gym, Olivia?
Olivia: The machines are all brand new, and it's only five minutes from my flat.
Gareth: Sounds perfect.
Olivia: It would be, but I can only go after work, and that's when everyone else goes. I usually have to wait ages to use anything. I might start going early in the morning instead.

Kirsty: Are you still cycling to work, Ian?
Ian: Every day. I thought it would take much longer than the car, but with all the traffic in the mornings, I actually get there ten minutes earlier.
Kirsty: Isn't it dangerous, though, on those busy roads?
Ian: There's a cycle path most of the way now, so I feel quite safe. And I'm not tired at all. I've got more energy than before.

Marcus: Since when do you do yoga, Holly?
Holly: Since January. My sister's been trying to get me to go with her for years, but I always said no.
Marcus: So what changed your mind?
Holly: Exams, really. I was so stressed I couldn't think properly. Someone told me yoga helps you relax, so I tried it. And it works. I feel much calmer now. My sister's really happy I'm there, of course!

Ruth: So, how's the no-sugar month going, Pete?
Pete: Well, I was sure I'd be desperate for chocolate after a couple of days. But honestly, I hardly think about it.
Ruth: Really? I'd find it impossible.
Pete: So did I! I haven't lost any weight yet, but that wasn't really why I did it. I just wanted to have more energy.

Woman: You've been out running every day this week, Max!
Max: It's this app. It gives you points for every kilometre, and you can see how your friends are doing. I'm trying to beat Lewis.
Woman: I thought you hated running.
Max: I did! But now it's like a game. And it was free, so you can't complain.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 3.
horenParts.transcript:
Man: Good morning. My name's Gareth Price, and I work for Hadley Town Council. I'm here to explain how our new bike-hire scheme works. It starts on the first of May.

Man: To begin with, there'll be fifteen places around Hadley where you can collect a bike. We're hoping to have thirty by next summer, so the scheme should grow quite quickly.

Man: Before you can hire a bike, you'll need to register. You can do this online, or, if you'd rather speak to someone, at the library on Market Street. Lots of people have asked about the town hall, but unfortunately you can't register there.

Man: The first thirty minutes of every journey are free. After that, you pay one pound for each hour, so an afternoon ride out into the countryside won't cost very much at all.

Man: All the bikes are bright green, and every one has a basket at the front, which is really useful if you're going shopping. They also have lights, so you can ride them safely after dark.

Man: We don't provide helmets, I'm afraid. But we strongly recommend wearing one, and you can buy a cheap one at the cycle shop inside the railway station.

Man: Finally, if anything's wrong with your bike, a flat tyre, for example, please return it to a stand and press the red button. That tells our team it needs repairing. The green button is only for unlocking the bike. Happy cycling!

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 4.
horenParts.transcript:
Interviewer: My guest today is Priya Shah, who taught English in Leeds for five years before moving to Chile, where she now works in a secondary school in the city of Valparaíso. Priya, why did you decide to move abroad?

Priya: People often ask if I went for the money, but actually I earn less now than I did in England. And no, I didn't follow a boyfriend there either! I'd simply been doing the same job in the same school for five years, and I felt I needed something new. A friend sent me the advert, and I thought, why not?

Interviewer: What did you find hardest when you first arrived?

Priya: I'd expected the language to be the big problem, but my Spanish actually improved quite quickly. What I found difficult was all the unwritten rules at school. For example, I didn't know how formally I should speak to the head teacher, or whether it was OK to leave the staff room before everyone else. It took me months to feel relaxed.

Interviewer: How are your students different from the ones you taught in England?

Priya: They're not that different, really. Teenagers are teenagers everywhere! But one thing I've noticed is that my students here are much less afraid of making mistakes. They'll just start speaking, even if their English isn't perfect. In England, students often waited until they were sure they were right.

Interviewer: Do teachers there work differently from teachers in the UK?

Priya: In some ways, yes. At first, to be honest, I thought my way of teaching was better. But I've changed my mind. My Chilean colleagues are brilliant at making lessons fun, and I'm probably better at organising things. We've learnt a lot from each other, and I've completely changed some of my lessons because of them.

Interviewer: How do you feel about being so far from your family?

Priya: Honestly, it's been much easier than I feared. We have a video call every Sunday, and my parents have already come to visit twice. The only time I find it really hard is at Christmas, when everyone's together at home and I'm on the other side of the world.

Interviewer: What advice would you give to teachers who are thinking about working abroad?

Priya: Some people say you should learn the language perfectly before you go, but I don't agree. You'll learn it much faster once you're there. My main advice would be to stay for at least two years. In the first year, you're just finding out how everything works. It's only in the second year that you really start to enjoy it.

Interviewer: Priya Shah, thank you very much.

schreibenParts.task:
Part 1. You must answer this question.

Read this email from your friend Ella and the notes you have made.

From: Ella
Subject: Our camping trip

Hi!

I've found a lovely campsite next to a lake for our trip on the weekend of 22 May. It's got a shop and a café, and you can hire canoes there! [Note 1: Sounds great!]

We can get there by train and walk from the station, or we can cycle all the way. It's about 30 kilometres. Which do you prefer? [Note 2: Say which and why]

We need to take some food for cooking on the campfire. What should we take? [Note 3: Suggest …]

My tent is quite small. Have you got a bigger one? [Note 4: No, but …]

Love,
Ella

Write your email to Ella using all the notes. Write about 100 words.

Part 2. Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question 2: Article
You see this notice in an English-language travel magazine.

ARTICLES WANTED!
A weekend in the countryside
Where would you go for a weekend in the countryside? What would you do there? Why do some people prefer the countryside to the city?
Write an article answering these questions. The best article will win a prize.

Write your article.

Question 3: Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story.
Your story must begin with this sentence:
'We could hear something moving outside the tent.'

Write your story.

sprechenParts.title: Part 1 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 1 (2-3 minutes). The examiner asks you some questions about yourself.

What's your name? Do you work or are you a student?
How often do you use your mobile phone?
What do you use the internet for?
Which app do you use most? Why?
Tell us about the first computer or phone you had.
Do you like playing computer games? Why / Why not?

sprechenParts.title: Part 2 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation: Part 2 (about 1 minute). Look at the photograph. It shows a grandmother and two teenagers sitting together on a sofa in a living room. One of the teenagers is holding a tablet and showing her something on the screen, and they are all laughing. Tell us what you can see in the photograph.

sprechenParts.title: Part 3 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 3 (2-3 minutes). Talk to your partner.

A family wants to spend a whole weekend without phones, computers or television. Here are some things they could do instead:

play board games
go for a bike ride
bake a cake together
visit a museum
camp in the garden
learn to play a musical instrument

Talk together about the different things the family could do, and say which would be the most enjoyable for the whole family.

sprechenParts.title: Part 4 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 4 (about 3 minutes). The examiner asks you and your partner some questions about technology and free time.

What do you like doing in your free time when you are not using a screen?
Do you think people spend too much time on their phones? Why / Why not?
How has technology changed the way families spend time together?
Is it a good idea to learn new skills from online videos? Why / Why not?
Would you find it difficult to live without the internet for a week? Why?
